headline: Cohasset police investigate hostage hoax that closed Route 3A
dek: A caller claimed two people were being held at gunpoint inside a Route 3A jewelry store, but officers found no hostages or injuries after a regional response.
body: Cohasset police are investigating a reported hostage emergency that turned out to be an elaborate hoax at a jewelry business on Route 3A Sunday evening. The [Cohasset Police Department statement published by Cohasset Anchor](https://cohassetanchor.com/cohasset-police-investigating-hoax-hostage-incident-at-route-3a-jewelry-store/) says the South Shore Regional Emergency Communications Center received the call at about 6:30 p.m. on Oct. 11. The male caller claimed he was inside the closed store with two hostages, said he had a pistol and a rifle, and demanded money for their release.

Dispatchers treated the report as a genuine, potentially life-threatening event and activated a Tac-Alert, a regional response that brought Cohasset officers together with on-duty police from Hingham, Norwell, Scituate and Hull. Officers established a perimeter around the business, while incoming mutual-aid units closed Route 3A in both directions between the Scituate town line and Beechwood Street. That closure temporarily affected a major South Shore route while police worked to determine whether anyone inside the store was in danger.

The caller made the threat harder to dismiss by describing police activity as it happened. According to the police account, he accurately described where responding officers were and provided details about employee-only areas inside the business. Those details initially made the report appear credible. They also led investigators to suspect that the caller was not simply guessing about the scene but had access to information that ordinary callers would not have had.

Police contacted the business owner, who confirmed that she and her family were safe. The owner also reached employees and confirmed that they were safe. Officers then entered the building and conducted a tactical sweep. They found no occupants and no evidence that a hostage situation had occurred. Police said no hostages were taken and no injuries were reported.

The department said the caller had apparently gained unauthorized access to the store’s video-surveillance system and used it to watch the police response in real time. That is an investigative conclusion described as apparent, not a public finding about how the system was accessed or who was responsible. Cohasset detectives are still working to identify the caller and examine the suspected surveillance intrusion. Police have not announced an arrest or criminal charges in the statement released Monday.

[NBC Boston’s report](https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/cohasset-mass-jewelry-store-hoax-call/4029924/) independently confirmed the main sequence of events and described the incident as “swatting,” the practice of making a false emergency report to provoke a large law-enforcement response at an unsuspecting location. The label explains why the incident matters beyond the store itself: a fabricated threat can put officers, business employees and bystanders into a fast-moving armed-response scenario, while emergency personnel are diverted from actual calls.

The response also shows how a local emergency can become regional within minutes. The Tac-Alert brought several departments into the operation, and the Route 3A closure created a public-safety buffer while dispatchers stayed on the phone with the caller. The police statement praised the dispatchers and mutual-aid partners, but the public record does not say how long the roadway was closed, whether the jewelry business sustained any damage, or whether the suspected surveillance access affected other systems.

The investigation remains open. Cohasset police said detectives will pursue the identification of the caller and appropriate criminal charges if the evidence supports them. Until then, the confirmed facts are limited to the emergency call, the coordinated police response, the temporary Route 3A closure, the building sweep and the absence of hostages or reported injuries. The apparent surveillance access is a central unanswered question, and officials have not released the name of the business or described a suspect.
